text:
卧槽，Google 和 Google DeepMind 最新放出了一篇很有意思的论文：Dream-RSI。

全称就是 Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Worlds，讲的是RSI（递归自我改进）。

但它做 RSI 的方式，和我们过去想象的不太一样。模型没有自己训练模型，也没有修改自己的权重，而是开始修改自己的「探索策略」。

简单来说，Agent 每次执行任务，都会留下完整的探索历史：试过哪些方案、哪些失败了、哪个分支效果最好、花了多少计算。

Dream-RSI 会把这些历史直接做成一个 Replay Simulator，然后让 Agent 在里面不断「做梦」：如果当时先走另一个分支呢？如果多开几个并行任务呢？如果这个方向早点停掉呢？

关键是，历史里的结果都已经算过了，所以这些实验根本不用重新调用 Coding Agent 和 Evaluator。

一次昂贵的真实探索，可以拿来做成千上万次几乎零执行成本的策略实验。

找到更好的策略之后，再把它部署回真实世界，于是就形成了一个完整循环：

探索 → 积累历史 → 做梦 → 改进 Policy → 再探索 → 再做梦。

一个 RSI Loop 就这么闭上了。

效果也很好啊，在 GPU Kernel 任务里，VGG16 和 LayerNorm 达到类似性能，分别少用了 2.43× 和 1.79× generations；
ConvDiv 和 ConvMax 在相近预算下，性能分别提高了 2.09× 和 1.44×。

还有一个实验我觉得特别有意思。

他们也试过更传统的办法：把过去探索得到的经验总结出来，直接塞回 Prompt 里指导下一轮，结果反而更差。

因为这些总结出来的「经验」很容易变成偏见，让 Agent 过早集中在某几个看起来正确的方向上，反而损失了探索的多样性。

所以这篇论文真正值得关注的地方，是它展示了另一条 RSI 路线：

模型不一定要先学会修改自己的权重，Agent 可以先学会修改自己的 Harness。

怎么搜索、开多少分支、什么时候继续、什么时候放弃、计算资源怎么分配，这些过去由人类工程师设计的东西，现在也开始进入 Agent 自己的优化循环。

底层还是同一个模型，但它开始自己研究：到底怎么用自己，才能变得更强。

text:
女生过了三十岁真的很难找对象了吗？

32岁，相亲见了三次，彼此都挺满意。

第三次吃完饭，男人忽然说：“你什么都挺好，就是我家里更希望我找个二十七八岁的，生孩子不用那么赶。”

text:
i turned GPT-6 Astra into a 24/7 trading agent

here is the EXACT way to build your FIRST AI trading bot with GPT-6 Astra with COMPLETE ARCHITECTURE

GPT-6 Astra is most powerful trading agent ever built

the goal was simple - ship hedge fund grade trading strategies with a multi-agent team of quants 

every layer solves one specific failure mode i hit in earlier versions:

1. reasoning substrate - GPT-6 Astra with 1M context, hours of long-horizon reasoning, direct computer use, and mathematical capabilities 

2. harness layer - AgenKit installs 10 specialist agents inside Codex CLI. Conductor, Backend Architect, Test Engineer, Code Reviewer, Data Engineer, Debugger, Frontend, Infra DevOps, Perf Observability, Security. same model, TEN DISCIPLINES 

3. workflow gates - 6 phases with operator approval at every step. brainstorm, architecture, plan, build, review, ship. nothing writes code until you sign off on the spec

4. mathematical foundation - 4 models running in production. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stat arb, Avellaneda-Stoikov market making, Hawkes order flow, Heston volatility

5. production architecture - 6 layers wrapping every strategy. data, signal, decision, risk, execution, monitoring. the 2 AM WebSocket disconnect can no longer silently kill the model

6. risk enforcement - Kelly-sized positions, 5% drawdown kill switches, delta-neutral hedging, intent blotter output. these numbers came from watching an earlier chatbot script blow through 12% in one session

7. validation gates - every strategy must pass Sharpe above 1.5, drawdown below 15%, hit rate above 55%, t-stat above 2.0, walk-forward across 5 years before any capital touches it

8. output layer - Telegram Bot pings my phone with instrument, strategy, Sharpe, drawdown, action window and Kelly-sized position

the principle i built around from day one

> capability without structure is a chatbot
> the wall was never the math, it was always the six salary team

i learned that one the hard way

every layer solves one specific failure mode i hit in earlier versions:

1. reasoning substrate - GPT-6 Astra with 1M context, hours of long-horizon reasoning, direct computer use, and mathematical capabilities 

2. harness layer - AgenKit installs 10 specialist agents inside Codex CLI. Conductor, Backend Architect, Test Engineer, Code Reviewer, Data Engineer, Debugger, Frontend, Infra DevOps, Perf Observability, Security. same model, TEN DISCIPLINES 

3. workflow gates - 6 phases with operator approval at every step. brainstorm, architecture, plan, build, review, ship. nothing writes code until you sign off on the spec

4. mathematical foundation - 4 models running in production. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stat arb, Avellaneda-Stoikov market making, Hawkes order flow, Heston volatility

5. production architecture - 6 layers wrapping every strategy. data, signal, decision, risk, execution, monitoring. the 2 AM WebSocket disconnect can no longer silently kill the model

6. risk enforcement - Kelly-sized positions, 5% drawdown kill switches, delta-neutral hedging, intent blotter output. these numbers came from watching an earlier chatbot script blow through 12% in one session

7. validation gates - every strategy must pass Sharpe above 1.5, drawdown below 15%, hit rate above 55%, t-stat above 2.0, walk-forward across 5 years before any capital touches it

8. output layer - Telegram Bot pings my phone with instrument, strategy, Sharpe, drawdown, action window and Kelly-sized position

the principle i built around from day one

> capability without structure is a chatbot
> the wall was never the math, it was always the six salary team

i learned that one the hard way

text:
加息 Quarter Point。
而且预期今年还会加一次息。
我个人的看法，一场超大规模的crisis，在天际边。
1.国债的利率最近破5%了。
Fed 不得不加0.25% 意思一下。
2.  现在的房贷利率已经到7.x%了。
2. 现在的商业贷款利息很多都已经快接近10%了。
unsecured  贷款利益都已经1x%了

整个市场上的资金成本非常非常高。
而这个是能通过加0.25%能解决的吗？
我不觉得。

房地产在美国大部分地区都冷了下来，西雅图地区一般都是滞后于全国水平的。最近几个月的数据也是一塌糊涂。
而且这个趋势是一路向下：
一轮又一轮的裁员压力。导致大家的信心变差。
高企的贷款利率，导致持有成本很高。
房价往下走的趋势很明显，卖房的人激增。 
虽然不会带来次贷危机，但是很显然会影响整个经济的增长。

油价
伊朗没有打服。
伊朗和小弟胡塞武装下狠手把也门给平推了，把沙特打的落花流水。
整个中东出现了一个控制波斯湾和红海的油霸。
沙特的输油管道也被伊朗给袭击了。
而美国现在没有打服伊朗的能力和计划。
伊朗硬生生把美国的国债利率顶到了5%。
这个高油价可能会维持很长一段时间。
高油价对欧美日韩中的经济会带来巨大的冲击。
冬天马上来了，欧洲这个冬天的取暖怎么办？

对于美国国内来讲，物流成本已经飙升了。
aka 今年跟去年比差不多增加了 43% 
So far in the third quarter, the index is up 43% y/y.
我们直接的体感也差不多。去年我们中远程inbound per pallet的cost大概在150-250之间，今年per pallet基本上没有低于200的了。

最后反应的就是通胀，以及工人工资的上涨。

另外一个慢慢暴露的危机是，AI 泡沫的破裂。
一个观察的例子就是Oracle，他all in AI。
但是现在他们挣扎在大裁员，创始人抛售巨额股票的阴影下。
这个可能还有待观察：就是AI投入巨大，即便毛利率巨高，但是无法真正创造出足够的价值，形成一个正向的循环。而且无法彻底拉开与开源模型的差距。
这个现在大家都在有怀疑，也有争论。
现在资金的成本上升之后，中东油佬的资金链出现问题，需要救急的时候，那么这个继续玩下去，能不能再玩下去就需要打个大大的问号。
而这个时候，Anthropic，openAI, XAI 声称需要减速，我个人认为不是道德，责任感，人类的危机感，让他们减速。
而是资金问题，以及这个游戏参与方对RoI的concern，导致的训练减速。

一旦这个泡沫破裂，那么美股将出现大幅下跌。

考虑美国政治的特点，
共和党不希望这个泡沫在28年前破灭。
这也能解释为啥Trump疯狂打call。
民主党希望这个泡沫在27年或者28年上半年破灭。
这样能把MAGA势力彻底扫除美国政坛。

那么，美国很有可能在27年到28年间，出现一次非常大规模的衰退。

所以，
需要一定控制自己的风险敞口，
控制自己的扩张速度，
控制自己的成本支出，人效。

悠着点，前几年那种房价涨，股价涨，消费涨，收入涨，营收涨的好日子，在美国也快到头了。

道理很简单，他爸爸就是京剧伴奏名家，他天天吃完晚饭，跟他爸爸去剧场，找个地方一坐，就是国家级的教学。

就这样从岁学到18岁，光自己边听边练，已经比戏校绝大多数教授强了， 已经日常跑出去给大师名家伴奏了。

你说你一个报考艺术类大学的臭傻逼，18岁连京剧都没接触过，一句都没听过，你怎么跟他竞争？

假如北京市京剧院招聘，今年招10个人，其中报名的就有300人，里面50人都跟这个邢木木一样，

你一个22岁刚刚能模模糊糊听懂戏词、一天台都没上过的大傻逼，你该如何跟他们如何去竞争？

We open sourced BrowserSkill, a bridge between your agent and your actual browser.

most tools give the agent a blank browser. We let it borrow a tab from yours, then hand it back.

> login state is already there, it just works where you're signed in
> captchas and confirmation dialogs come back to you, then it continues
> it's a CLI, not an MCP server => any agent that can run a shell can use it, and you see every call it makes

one thing that's easy to miss: the agent asks before borrowing a tab, and that switch lives in your browser settings, not in a flag, so it can't be talked around.

one line to install, works with Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, Openclaw, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy. Everything runs locally, MIT.

https://t.co/LBOjW8rxXp

用过 Codex / ChatGPT Work 的人都懂，额度说撞就撞。官方没有公开 reset 日历，全靠 @thsottiaux 不定时发推。你刚起势写代码，额度见底；刷完 X 才发现昨天已经 reset 过了，或者干等三天什么都没有。焦虑不是功能缺失，是「信息不同步」。

这个站就干一件事：把 Tibo 的重置公告扒下来，做成公开时间线——上次什么时候 reset、隔了多久、原文怎么说。用户打开看一眼就走，跳出率大约 74%，人均 1.6 页，停留三分钟左右。对工具站来说，这恰恰说明需求打准了：不是留你玩，是给你答案。

流量是怎么起来的？👇

text:
Today we rolled out Astra to every engineer at Databricks (N=~3500). Some notes that may be helpful to others:

1. Astra unambiguously out performs our previous highest-end models (Opus 5, Sol 5.6) on highly complex tasks, especially those related to high level system design or long range horizontal tasks.

2. Engineers given Astra increased overall coding spend by around 60% compared to baseline.

3. It is not clear Astra meaningfully improves on medium/low complexity coding tasks compared to earlier models. We suspect those tasks are mostly saturated (i.e. perfectly executed) by existing models.

4. We learned above by piloting Astra with around 200 users to gain signal on both quality and cost. We use Unity Gateway to do cohort-based experiments for all new models.

5. We give engineers a sub-budget specific to Astra to encourage them to use Astra selectively on complex tasks while preferring lower cost models for everyday tasks. Our engineers are able to mix-and-match tools and models within their overall budget envelope (we also allow for increased budgets through various mechanisms). These budgets are defined in Unity Gateway and regularly revisited.

Note: We do not have robust comparisons of Astra-vs-Fable because we have net yet rolled out Fable widely due to data retention policies.

text:
For anyone curious how Jev works, I made a visual explanation using @claudeai :)

This is based on the Qwen2.5-RLCD model which @harshagundal released on @huggingface 

The idea is to replace autoregressive LLM generation by a single Transformer decoder (of a pre-trained LLM), which processes the context + JSON schema only once. The keys and values of those tokens are cached.

Next, for each field of the JSON schema, we:
1. pass its field suffix tokens through the Transformer decoder again (reusing the KV-cache)
2. obtain a final hidden state, which we pass through the language modeling head
3. we obtain scores, also called logits, for all tokens in the vocab of the LLM
4. we only look at the scores of the tokens we care about for the given field, and pass those through a softmax to obtain probabilities which sum to 1
5. we take the token with the highest probability.

The benefits of this are that:
1. it's fast (we don't need to generate the JSON schema token by token)
2. it's 100% valid JSON (we don't need to rely on the model to generate a valid schema)

text:
很多人现在喜欢Vibe Coding，
一行代码不看，甚至连VS Code都懒得开，项目需求一通口喷，问题甩给 AI 咔咔咔咔咔的干，感觉爽爆了

但这种方式往往会导致一个巨大的问题，到了项目的中期， 软件里全是bug
而这个时候你的AI已经制造了一坨 10万 行代码的屎山， 此时不管是最强的 GPT6 Astra 还是Claude Fable5.1都没有办法维护下去，修一个bug 出 3个bug 。
而此时作为这个项目的唯一负责人你，对项目一无所知，也不愿意再从头把前面产生的屎山理顺一遍 
于是项目就彻底被废弃了 
这不是一个少有的现象，在项目的规模大到10万行这种级别的时候，几乎一定会出现这种问题

text:
一个人对王石的态度，代表着他的认知。前几天在北京 HYROX 现场，我就站在赛道护栏边上。

75 岁的王石从我身边冲过去，上半身微佝偻，每一根肋骨都在剧烈起伏，汗水直接甩在地胶上。

坦白说，那一秒我被震住了。

那一刻我脑子里闪过的，不是万科，不是地产恩怨，不是八卦热搜。

而是老家那些 75 岁的老人——

多数人早已坐进轮椅，或者在老宅屋檐下发呆等死，生活难以自理。

而这个身家数亿的老人，75 岁，不混酒局，在世界标准的体能竞技场里把自己逼到生理极限。

身旁的田朴珺在嘶吼助威。

旁人眼里是“秀”，我眼里只有近乎残酷的“生命力”。

text:
9/16 今天股市里最大的消息是美联储加息落地,  加息25bp，利率来到3.75%–4.00%，12比0通过

美联储发言相当鹰派, 我一点不意外。我认为，其实真正精彩的是在加息舞台背后的博弈和算计

因为每次下跌都是一次机会。你说为什么？我来说个故事剧本, 大家看有没有道理？

以下是剧本：

大家先假设我在上学，我希望班长少布置一点作业。

我暗地里花钱打点，扶持了我的小弟当了班长。

最聪明的方式其实不是上来让我的小弟就对我表忠心，

于是我跟他决定商量演一台戏。让他越强硬、越独立越好，最好跟我反着干

我每天当着全班的面高喊：“作业太多了，根本做不完，我要减少作业！”

班长大声斥责我说：“为了整个班集体的学习成绩，我一定要多布置点作业。”

但还是有人指指点点，说他就是我的小弟，直到班长真的把作业越布置越多，大家也就渐渐闭嘴了

但是呢，班长同时也说，要不要布置作业还要看数据，看整体班级的成绩。这个我无法为全体同学做更多的保证

到后来，班长确实加了几次作业，树立起了威信。

再后来，班长不管做什么有利于我的事情，不论是减作业、给我特权，大家都不会再认为我和他之间有利益关系了

所以连他们自己都认为Gemini不好用，还有谁会用Gemini。

Gemini的营收和用户数量都是Google虚拟出来的，本质上是其他服务的客户强行划分为Gemini用户，原本的云或者搜索不得不额外提供AI服务。

text:
A 118K-star GitHub repo is built around one painfully obvious idea:

Your coding agent should map the codebase once, not grep it forever.

Graphify turns an entire project into a queryable knowledge graph.

Functions, classes, files, SQL schemas, infrastructure, docs, PDFs, images and videos become connected nodes that an agent can traverse instead of repeatedly opening files and reconstructing the architecture.

So instead of:
→ search for authentication
→ open twelve files
→ follow imports manually
→ lose the trail as the context fills up

The agent can ask:
> What connects authentication to the database?
> Trace the path from UserService to DatabasePool.
> Explain RateLimiter.
> Which concepts does everything flow through?

Graphify returns the relevant subgraph and the path connecting the concepts, not another list of keyword matches.

For source code, this is not RAG:
→ No embeddings
→ No vector database
→ No LLM required
→ Code is parsed locally using tree-sitter
→ Calls, imports and inheritance become graph edges

Every relationship is also marked as EXTRACTED, INFERRED, or AMBIGUOUS, so the agent can distinguish what exists explicitly in the source from what Graphify resolved or guessed.

The cleverest part is what happens next.

Graphify can install hooks or persistent instructions for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot and 20+ other assistants.

Before the agent starts blindly grepping or reading files one by one, it is nudged to query the existing graph first.

The graph can be committed to Git, automatically rebuilt after commits, shared across the team and exposed through MCP.

Long context windows help agents read more code.

A persistent knowledge graph helps them know where to look.

The next improvement in coding agents may not come from stuffing more files into the prompt.

It may come from making them stop rereading the repository.

Here's the GitHub Repo: https://t.co/4ify3X8urp

text:
🔥 Excited to share that #paper2agent is published in @Nature today!  

Papers have long been the primary format for communicating scientific knowledge, but they remain static. Putting that knowledge to work requires connecting findings to data, navigating supplementary materials, and adapting methods to new questions - effort repeated by each new reader.  

We introduce Paper2Agent, a multi-agent framework that automatically turns research papers into virtual authors. Paper2Agent turns a paper’s manuscript, code, data, and supplements into an MCP server that any AI agent can access, with automated testing and iterative refinement in an agentic loop. The paper then becomes a virtual author you can talk to: trace claims to evidence, analyze your own data, and collaborate with other papers’ virtual authors  

Agentifying a paper turns it from something people read into something people and AI agents can discover and build on - providing the context needed to interpret its findings and reuse its methods reliably. We tested how reliably these agents put papers to use. Across multiple benchmarks, agents created by Paper2Agent outperformed baselines such as Claude Code working directly with papers' PDFs and code repositories.  

Once papers become virtual authors, they can collaborate - much like human researchers do. In one case study, agents built from AlphaGenome and two large-scale genetic perturbation studies worked together to propose a new computational approach for integrating evidence across different perturbation datasets. By connecting predictions from one paper with experimental data from others, they helped pinpoint a likely causal gene for psoriasis.  

We hope Paper2Agent makes scientific knowledge easier to access, reuse, and build on - a first step toward a future where millions of paper agents proactively collaborate with human researchers and one another to advance discovery.  

🤖Talk to the virtual author for Paper2Agent itself: https://t.co/wCzxUS4alX
📎Paper: https://t.co/2EGOPUgirB
💻Code: https://t.co/290bZWDmRt 

VERY grateful to work with this incredible team: @james_y_zou, @jkpritch, Yaohui, and Joe!

A great idea I'm stealing from @dexhorthy:

When you first start building a software factory, make it TINY.

Don't get it to triage every issue in your repo. Just do one per day.

Check its output. Adjust it. Keep going with your regular work.

As you begin to trust its judgment, get it to triage TWO issues per day instead. Then five. Then ten.

Start small. Adjust. Build trust. Expand.

His second spring has arrived because he made the right decision for his career in the summer. It is actually quite similar to Tadić, who has an exceptional talent as well, but fell just short of playing for a top-tier team but could be pure class in a smaller league, in a setup that allowed him to play at his best.

text:
Claude Code 团队自己，已经有 70~80% 的工作不在终端里做了。

看完 Thariq、Sid、Robert 三个人的 22 分钟对谈，记了几条。

1. 大部分活在 Slack 里的 Claude Tag 上干。TUI 和桌面端只有两种时候才开，精修某个东西，或者"想微观管理我的那些 Claude"。给的也不再是任务，是目标。

2. 以前底层技术的保质期以年计，现在是两个月。Sonnet 3.5 时代模型给它五件事只做三件就放弃，于是加了 to-do list，一下就好了。一年后这个功能没了，因为不需要了。Sid 的结论是对自己造的东西不要有感情。

3. harness 里大部分功能，说白了是在给当前模型的失败模式打补丁。模型变强就主动删。但任务尺度同时在变大，又得造形态完全不同的新工具。这两句得一起记，只记前一句就是为删而删。

4. AskUserQuestion 这个工具磨了很久才让模型学会调用。结果作者现在自己都不怎么用了，直接让 Claude 出一个带 mockup 的 artifact 来问他问题。

5. Code review 变了。人类 reviewer 挑三个小 nitpick，其实是在证明"我读了"。这活交给 Claude。人只管 Claude 不知道的事，这个 API 为什么长这样，服务边界为什么画在这。

6. workflows 是从 code review 长出来的。fan out 找 bug，每个 bug 再从几个角度对抗性验证，过滤掉误报只留真的。Robert 信任 workflows 的理由很简单，编排层是代码，for 循环不会漏掉任何一项。

7. Claude Tag 第一次把界面和 transcript 彻底分开。Slack 里看到的每条消息都是它主动调工具发的，内心独白看不到。他们一开始很慌，后来发现不盯着也能拿到好结果，才意识到模型真的到这一步了。

8. 怀念什么？Sid 怀念性能优化，"现在 Claude 比我强得多"。Robert 曾经花一整天手写 CSS 复刻 Mac OS 10.4 的 Aqua 按钮，叠了好几层 radial gradient。他说再也不会手工做这种事了。听着有点唏嘘。

text:
在机器学习和信息论中，有一个著名的直觉叫流形假说。

现实世界产生的数据，在名义上往往拥有极高维度：一张高清图片可能对应数百万个像素维度，自然语言、声音、蛋白质序列、行为轨迹也都存在于极其庞大的状态空间中。

但有意义的数据并不会均匀散落在这些空间里，它会被压缩在一个极小、极其特殊的结构区域中。
一张随机生成的百万像素图片几乎不可能恰好构成一张真实人脸，因为自然图像同时受到身份、姿态、光照、透视、物体结构和物理规律等大量约束。
流形，只是这种低复杂度结构的一种几何表达，更一般地说，机器学习真正能够成立，是因为现实世界的数据根本不是随机噪声。

这也是理解智能最重要的起点。
智能存在的第一条件，在于这个世界必须具有可预测结构。
假如一个宇宙中的未来和过去完全独立，那么无论是人脑、Transformer还是无限大的超级计算机，都无法通过观察过去提高对未来的预测，因为这个世界根本没有留下任何可以学习的规律。
白噪声无法被理解，也无法被预测。
因此，智能能够存在，本身就意味着宇宙不是最大随机性的混沌，而包含大量跨尺度稳定的统计依赖、几何约束、组合结构、动力学规律和因果关系。

从这个角度看，机器学习做的事情是在巨量观测中寻找可以压缩的规律。
模型看过十亿张人脸，并不需要在参数里存储十亿份像素副本，它需要形成的是关于身份、轮廓、姿态、光照、空间关系等潜在变量的生成结构，最终用一个远短于全部训练数据本身的模型去近似。
因此，Learning在很深的意义上就是Compression。
如果一个庞大的数据集合能够被一个更短的生成程序描述，那么模型获得的就是规律。这与Kolmogorov Complexity的直觉高度一致。
生成或描述这些数据所需的最短程序究竟有多长，是一个重要的问题。

但是，数据不均匀本身仍然不足以产生智能。一个变量即使99%的概率取0、1%的概率取1，它的分布极度不均匀，却未必具有任何复杂结构。
重要的是变量之间存在可以利用的依赖。知道 (X) 之后，是否能够减少对 (Y) 的不确定性，这才是信息。
Mutual Information (I(X;Y)) 所度量的，本质上正是这种关系。
所以，智能依赖的是世界内部存在稳定的dependency；
统计规律、几何结构、层级结构、因果关系以及时间上的连续性共同构成了学习能够发生的基础。

这也给出了理解大模型的一种更准确方式。
一个随机初始化的神经网络最初只是一个巨大的、没有意义的函数族，而梯度下降不断利用数据排除那些与现实分布不一致的函数。
经过海量训练之后，原本随机的参数逐渐形成高度结构化的内部表征。
语言结构、空间关系、人物与概念关系、程序结构和部分物理规律也进入其中。

这里，我们不能简单说神经网络与现实世界同构。因为同构是一个过于严格的数学概念。
其实，模型是在自己的计算介质中形成了一套能够保存现实世界部分稳定关系的内部表示。
它是世界结构在另一种介质中的压缩投影。

于是，所谓智能涌现也没有那么神秘。
如果模型只能捕捉局部统计相关性时，它表现为模式匹配；
当它能够形成更长程、更抽象、更稳定的表示时，就出现泛化；
当不同领域的内部结构能够被重新组合，就表现为类比和联想；
当模型能够利用已有结构，对训练数据中没有直接出现过的状态进行推断，就表现为推理。

记忆、泛化、类比和推理，只是同一种机制在不同尺度上的表现：利用一个内部世界模型，在未观测区域重建结构。
模型规模之所以重要，是因为复杂世界需要足够大的函数空间才能被表示。
而某些能力的突然涌现，有时只是评价指标造成的阈值效应，有时也可能对应grokking或内部表示重组这样的真实非线性变化。
我想，我们需要更多地去关注参数空间在学习过程中发生了什么结构重组，使新的计算能力成为可能。

如果继续把这个问题推到信息论和统计物理层面，会得到更加统一的图景。
生命，依靠持续消耗自由能维持自身远离热平衡，而大脑和机器同样需要消耗能量进行信息处理。
由于Shannon entropy和热力学熵并不是同一个概念，我们可以更准确地定义，智能系统不断丢弃与任务无关的变化，同时保存对于预测和行动有价值的信息。

这与Information Bottleneck极其接近。
内部表示并不需要保存输入的一切，而只需要保留足够多能够预测未来、指导行为的结构。高级智能的标志，是知道什么必须留下，什么可以被遗忘。

由此，智能可以粗略地被写成Compression、Prediction、Control。
Compression意味着从海量观察中提取规律，Prediction意味着利用这些规律推断尚未看到的世界，Control意味着利用预测去改变未来。
一个有限的系统面对一个远比自身复杂的宇宙，通过观察世界、压缩世界、建立内部模型，再依靠这个模型预测并干预世界，这就是智能最一般的形式。

text:
Anthropic 工程师讲了一堂 FDE 入门课 
https://t.co/kakqFy0ZGZ

Kevin Bai 现在在 Anthropic 的 Applied AI 团队，之前是 Rippling FDE 团队的创始成员，再之前在 Palantir 干了好几年。最近他做了一个 FDE 101 的分享，把前线部署工程师这个角色讲得很清楚，值得总结一下。

先说一个数据：在上市 SaaS 公司里，按平均合同金额排，Palantir 是 400 万美元，ServiceNow 120 万，Workday 60 万，剩下的没有一家能超过 50 万。Palantir 靠几千人做到了别人几万人做不到的客单价。靠的就是 FDE 模式。

FDE 到底在解决什么问题？

Palantir 的产品 Foundry 是一个应用构建平台，技术门槛很高，但买家是石油、消费品这些行业的非技术高管。你把一个复杂的技术平台丢给一个不会写代码的人，指望他自己搞明白怎么用，这不现实。

所以 Palantir 的做法是：客户买的既不是软件产品，也不是咨询服务，而是一个"结果"。你派工程师过去，深入理解客户的业务场景，在平台上给他们把东西建出来。客户关心的是货架上多了多少商品、产线效率提升了多少，他们不关心数据怎么组织的，也不该关心。

FDE 和外包开发有什么区别？

Kevin 特别强调了一点：如果你的工程师每次都从零给客户写定制代码，那你做的不是 FDE，是外包开发。FDE 模式能成立，前提是你有一个可复用的平台。工程师是在平台已有的基础能力上组装和定制，不是每次重新造轮子。没有平台，维护成本会吞掉所有利润，工程师也会因为要维护几十个毫无关联的代码库而跑路。

要不要搞 FDE？两个问题就能判断。

第一，你是不是必须把一个技术复杂的东西卖给非技术买家？如果你的客户本身就是工程师，比如卖 GitHub 或者 Datadog 的，不需要 FDE。如果你的产品本身就是开箱即用的，比如 Slack 或者 Jira，也不需要。只有你的产品很复杂、客户又不懂技术的时候，FDE 才有必要。

第二，你有没有一个可复用的平台？或者你愿不愿意投入去建一个？没有共享的基础组件，FDE 就是不可持续的。

2026 年的新变化是什么？

Kevin 的判断很有意思：软件行业做生意的方式本身变了，AI 让构建软件变得极其容易，几乎所有平台都在走向 Agent 化，这意味着几乎所有平台都变得高度可定制。后果就是：越来越多的客户搞不清楚你的产品到底能做什么。你把产品的成败交给客户自己去摸索，在 Agent 时代会越来越难走通。

这就把 FDE 从 Palantir 独有的小众玩法，变成了更多软件公司需要认真考虑的事情。

最后一个问题：什么样的人适合做 FDE？

Kevin 的回答很简洁：FDE 就是一个你信任到可以让他直接面对客户的软件工程师。技术能力是基本盘，但你还得放心让他代表公司去跟客户打交道。

CoreWeave 今天点亮了全球首个英伟达 Vera Rubin NVL72 的多机柜（Multi-rack）集群。

正好对照看一眼今天的异动榜：CRDO、SMTC、COHR、LITE、MRVL 这批做光互联和 DSP 的厂，集体暴涨了 5% 到 8%。

NVL72 刚出的时候一直被叫作「全铜机柜」，当时市场很慌，觉得它会彻底杀掉光模块的逻辑。结果现在真实的 Multi-rack 一落地，老黄确实在单个机柜内部用铜线省了光，但只要你的算力规模逼着你把这些怪物机柜连起来，跨机柜的光互联需求直接是指数级的。

至于今天这走势，手里也没具体的资金流向数据，只能瞎猜一下：估计不少是当初因为纯铜机柜被洗出去的资金，这会儿又跑回来买了吧。

黄仁勋今天在一个公开峰会上，贡献了一个能载入科技圈史册的牛逼瞬间。

台下观众瞬间炸锅。
更绝的是，他接起电话直接来了一句：“总统先生，要不是因为您的电话，我这会儿还在台上跟大伙聊着呢“

Today's inflation data, largely in-line with consensus expectations, but still well above the Fed's target, is a reminder rising prices will still be a major issue for investors & voters in this midterm election cycle. 🗳️

But what comes after the midterms is what long-term investors should try to stay focused on. Since 1938, the 12 months following a midterm has always generated positive returns for the S&P 500. It's less about who wins and more about lifting the cloud of uncertainty - the purple haze as I like to call it - that may be hanging over markets.

We expect the headline noise to get louder the closer we get to the election, so what's an investor do to?! Stay diversified and buckle up, because there's typically volatility heading into November. But soon enough it'll all be in the rearview mirror!

My latest @PNCBank Adding Alpha breaks it down.

玛德，天下苦 Typeless 久矣！网易这次真憋了个大善人产品啊！

Typeless 免费额度从每周 8000 砍到 2000 字，关键是它最近还降智、过度修改，我就是那个 144$ 年费的大冤种。

我把主流输入法都测了，没找到好用的平替，对比如下图。但最近体验网易的叭哥说，真有点 UU 远程的感觉了。

而且终身免费，形态和 Typeless 一致，速度比 Typeless 快太多了，太tmd良心了！

实测下来的感觉：
1、非流式输入，说完松手直接输出排版分段好的文字，口水词去掉了，但语气还是在的。
2、超低音也准确，30dB 也能精准识别，和我之前连麦克风一样，户外用起来也很爽。
3、并且带 100+ 语种实时互译，同时也能自己加专业词库。
4、数据全在本地，云端不留存。

text:
NFL DFS: WEEK 2

A first look at this week's massive 13 game slate 

CIN🐯 AT HOU🐂

Chase Brown saw 20 touches in Week 1, including six targets, but $6,900 feels a little rich against a Texans defense that just held James Cook to 69 yards on 16 touches.

David Montgomery is more interesting at $6,500 after handling 23 Texans RB opportunities in his debut. Tampa's backs averaged nearly 5 yards per carry against Cincinnati last week.

Ja'Marr Chase is a bounce-back candidate after just 5-71 combined with Tee Higgins. Nico Collins also stands out after seeing double-digit targets in Week 1.

CLE 🟤AT TB🏴‍☠️

The Browns looked rough in Week 1, and I'm not interested in forcing their skill players into consideration until something changes.

Bucky Irving is much more appealing. He handled 15 touches, including seven receptions, and costs just $6,100 against a Browns team that should give Tampa opportunities to control the game.

Emeka Egbuka is interesting at $6,400, although he'll probably need some touchdown variance to get there. Tampa Bay DST is also firmly on the radar after Deshaun Watson took five sacks and turned the ball over last week.

PIT🟡 AT NE🟦

This doesn't immediately look like a game I want to attack.

The Patriots lost AJ Brown to IR, which should create more opportunity for Romeo Doubs, Mack Hollins, and Hunter Henry.

DK Metcalf saw 10 targets in Week 1 and is only $5,200. With pricing tightening up, that's enough to get my attention.

GB🧀 AT NYJ✈️

Breece Hall saw 24 touches in Week 1 and costs just $6,200. I expect another heavy workload.

Garrett Wilson continues to operate as the clear alpha, seeing more than twice as many targets as any other Jet. He's another player I could see getting plenty of exposure to.

On the other side, Matthew Golden was one of the biggest surprises of Week 1, seeing 12 targets. At $4,700, he's immediately interesting.

CAR🐈‍⬛ AT ATL🪶

Bijan Robinson is the most expensive player on the slate at $8,200, but he handled 31 opportunities in Week 1 and accounted for basically the entire Atlanta offense.

After watching D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai combine for 200 rushing yards against Carolina, I have a hard time ignoring Bijan in this spot.

Bryce Young is also intriguing at $5,400 after throwing for 361 yards and three TDs. Chuba Hubbard and Jalen Coker are both firmly in the conversation after strong Week 1 performances.

PHI🦅 AT TEN⚔️

Saquon Barkley only saw 15 carries and two targets in Week 1, but the Titans just looked overwhelmed defensively against the Jets.

At $7,000, he's an interesting pivot from Derrick Henry, who will likely attract plenty of attention in his matchup with New Orleans.

Nothing else immediately stands out through the air.

NO⚜️ AT BAL🐦‍⬛

This is my early favorite for game of the week.

Tyler Shough attempted 56 passes in Week 1 and now costs just $5,300. The Saints' passing game is extremely concentrated around Chris Olave and DeVaughn Vele, with Juwan Johnson adding another cheap piece at $3,900.

On the other side, Lamar Jackson is expensive at $7,300, but the matchup and rushing upside are obvious.

Derrick Henry is also difficult to ignore after 163 total yards and three TDs in Week 1. Zay Flowers is the situation to monitor after leaving with a hamstring injury.

MIN🟪 AT CHI🐻

The final early game gives us the biggest question mark: Kyler Murray's concussion status.

The Bears just scored nearly 60 points, so there are plenty of ways this game could get interesting.

I'd rather play Tyler Shough or Bryce Young at a cheaper price than Trevor Lawrence at $5,800 against Denver.

LV ☠️AT LAC⚡️

Ashton Jeanty saw 29 touches in Week 1 and led the Raiders in both rushing and receiving yards. At $6,800, I'm interested.

I'm taking a wait-and-see approach with Omarion Hampton after just 12 carries and zero targets.

If Brock Bowers remains out, I'm probably avoiding the Raiders passing game.

Ladd McConkey was off to a strong start before leaving with a rib injury. If he's out, Quentin Johnston and Tre Harris become interesting salary savers.

WAS⛑️ AT DAL🤠

This could be one of the games that gets overlooked after both teams lost in Week 1.

Terry McLaurin still played 87% of Washington's snaps despite the quiet fantasy day, and a Jayden Daniels + Stefon Diggs + McLaurin stack costs just $16,800.

That's a pretty interesting starting point.

On the Dallas side, Javonte Williams handled 17 touches and CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens remain the obvious pieces.

Chig Okonkwo is another name to monitor depending on his status after Likely's performance against Dallas.

SEA🟢 AT ARI🐦

Jaxon Smith-Njigba dominated Seattle's receiving work in Week 1 and is now the most expensive WR on the slate at $8,100.

He's still in play every week.

The Seattle RB situation is less appealing, although Jadarian Price could see more work with extra preparation time and Drew Lock under center.

Trey McBride and Michael Wilson remain interesting on the Arizona side.

MIA🐬 AT SF⛏️

This is the game that immediately jumps out as a potential spot for San Francisco to score five TDs.

Christian McCaffrey is $8,000 and is coming off a matchup where Ashton Jeanty just posted 100+ rushing yards, 45 receiving yards, and two TDs against Miami.

That's enough to put CMC firmly on the radar.

Brock Purdy is also interesting at $6,200, while Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, and George Kittle all become more appealing if we're building around the San Francisco offense.

On the Miami side, Caleb Douglas and Malik Washington are both cheap volume plays after seeing seven and eight targets respectively in Week 1.

That's where I'm at on the first look.

It's Monday.

A lot will change between now and Sunday.

True or False? Check now

Today @NoetiveAI (https://t.co/UquiHJiLDf) is emerging from stealth with $41 million in seed funding, founded by @Amirfrenkel and @DanBarak. We are building the Intelligence of Record for the Physical Economy.

AI has transformed information work. It has not yet transformed the $30 trillion physical economy: the factories, fleets, and job sites where thousands of variables change every day and the knowledge that matters most still lives in one person's head.

At Noetive, we are building the Intelligence of Record for the physical economy. A ‘brain’ – a self-improving AI that learns how a business truly runs and works alongside its team. It also includes the ‘eyes & ears’ – an advanced multi-modal sensing pod, a device that expands the brain's ability to perceive and reason about the environment and the business.

We are already in the field partnering and working closely with design partners across manufacturing & logistics.

We built this company with some of the best venture firms, operators, entrepreneurs and builders that joined us for this journey

A huge thank you to our partners at @EclipseVentures , @craft_ventures, @TheWestlyGroup, Swish Ventures, FactoryHQ, @gigascale, @incitedotorg , @Liquid2V , Operator Partners, @boztank , @Ahmad_Al_Dahle , @MattLRogers, Yaser Sheikh, @schrep, @bsofman,  @DLeitersdorf, @OLeitersdorf, @makavy, @MosheSshalev, @Casspi18 , @orristr989, @SteveWestly , @Mike_Rob_Craft , @taylordurand_ ,  for your support, guidance and companionship.

We are hiring AI researchers and full-stack AI-native engineers who want to take frontier research into the real world.

🇨🇦Mark Carney Signs Canada’s DEATH WARRANT:

Under Liberal Prime Minister Mark Carney’s leadership, Canada has announced that it plans to become an “Associate Member” of the European Union, with the consequences for everyday Canadians set to be absolutely catastrophic:

➡️Zero Vote in Brussels:

As an “Associate Member” of the European Union, Canada will be obligated to implement EU legislation without actually having a vote in Brussels during the decision-making process. Similar to how Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein currently operate, Canada will ikely lbe forced to implement product, climate, digital, and labour standards written by 27 countries that do not answer to Canadian voters – in almost all cases, with EU laws taking precedence over Canadian legislation.

➡️Increased Taxes:

Canadian tax revenue (including social contributions) currently stands at 34.9% of total Canadian GDP, while that figure sits at a shocking 39.4%, on average, in the European Union. As a consequence of adopting EU “Associate Member” status, individual Canadians are likely to experience an increased tax burden of about 13%.

➡️Increased Censorship:

As an “Associate Member” of the European Union, Canada is expected to adopt the European Union’s “Digital Services Act” model of internet censorship – embracing fines and criminal penalties for engaging in “hate speech,” as defined by the bureaucrats in Brussels.

➡️Increased Immigration:

Canada is expected to adopt a free-movement policy with all EU member nations after becoming an EU “Associate Member.” This means that any legal resident of the EU will also have the capacity to legally immigrate to Canada, should they so choose. Canada, a country with 41 million residents, is already facing the developed world’s most extreme housing and employment shortages. The Liberal Carney government has expressed a desire to import 765,000 “legal” immigrants per year.

text:
HOW TO DO AUTOMATE YOUR BUSINESS PART 2:

i drew up this master plan for myself in 2019.

Since then, I have pursued automating all my businesses as much as possible.

This is one of them. The flow is usually pretty similar for each one.

I mapped out the marketing system for Gymnastics Tools years ago. Classic content, SEO, and email. The boring stuff that supposedly doesn't work anymore.

But this machine just runs. It's an asset that quietly brings in new coaches every week without me touching it.

You can build and automate it piece by piece.

It’s the only way to manage multiple projects (for me). Build systems that compound, without you being around.

Let me know what you want to know more about.

looking forward to share more insights about it

quotedTweet.text:
a lot of people asked me today how I can go on holiday so often while my businesses keep running without me.

And judging by the replies, quite a few people were especially interested in the email marketing part of it.

So here's how it actually works for me.

1. GET TRAFFIC

First, you need traffic.

You can get that through:

• Social media
• Advertising
• SEO

I personally focus heavily on SEO.
I create useful content and then repurpose it.

A video → transcript → blog post → snippets → more content → more traffic.

The goal is to keep feeding the top of the funnel.

↓

2. TURN TRAFFIC INTO LEADS

Traffic alone isn't enough.

You need a way to turn visitors into people you can keep helping.

That's where lead magnets come in.

Create something genuinely useful that people actually want.

They exchange their email address for it.

ABOUT LEADMAGNETS

a lead magnet doesn't have to be a 50 page ebook.

It can be:

• A checklist
• A template
• A calculator
• A swipe file
• A video
• A collection of examples
• A useful spreadsheet
• A step by step guide
• Or simply something you've already built that saves someone else time.
• it can even just be a free tools platform / saas

The key is simple:
Make something people actually want.
Don't create a lead magnet because every marketing guru told you that you need one.

Create something that solves a real problem.

Now you have permission to keep providing value.

THE FIRST EMAIL

The first email is important too.

I confirm what they signed up for, but I also introduce myself.

- Who am I?
- Why should they listen to me?
- What can they expect?

And most importantly:

Give them value immediately.

Don't just say:

"Thanks for downloading."

Give them a reason to think:

"Okay, this was actually worth signing up for."

↓

3. GIVE A LOT OF VALUE

This is where I think most people get email marketing wrong.

I send emails.

A lot of them.

But every email needs to contain real value.

I actually want every email to hurt a little bit when I hit send.

Because I'm giving away something that could easily have been paid content.

That's intentional.

The more value you consistently give away, the more people think:

"Okay, this guy actually knows what he's talking about."

"I've learned a lot from him."

"I wonder what else he can help me with."

↓

4. TELL STORIES

This is a big one.

Most of my emails aren't:

"Here are 5 tips for doing X."

I tell stories.

Things I've actually experienced.

Things that went well.

Things that went terribly.

Mistakes I've made.

Experiments that worked.

Experiments that failed.

Things I'm currently figuring out.

And I'm honest about what isn't working.

You can teach someone a lesson in three sentences.

But wrap that lesson inside a real story and people remember it.

You can even talk about the weather today and hook it to your product or customers problem.

People follow people.

Not companies.

So I try to be as open and honest as I'm comfortable being.

I don't want every email to sound like it was written by a marketing department.

I want it to sound like me.

↓

5. WRITE LIKE A HUMAN

I use the person's first name.

Something as simple as:

"Hey Sarah,"

That's it.

I write very informally.

I write as if I'm writing to a friend.

Not "the subscriber".

Not "our valued customer".

One person.

I also care a lot about readability.

I don't write huge paragraphs.

I use lots of spacing.

Short sentences.

One thought per line.

It should almost feel like someone is talking to you.

↓

6. DON'T SEND A "NEWSLETTER"

I don't really think of it as a newsletter.

I don't want people to feel like they're subscribing to another company newsletter that arrives every Tuesday.

They're following me.

My businesses.

The things I'm building.

The things I'm learning.

The things that work.

And the things that don't.

So I don't put:

"Newsletter #47"

in the subject line.

I write subject lines that make the right person curious enough to open.

Because the best email in the world is useless if nobody opens it.

↓

7. MIX UP THE FORMAT

Not every email should look the same.

Sometimes:

• A blog post
• A video
• A personal story
• A lesson from my business
• Something that went wrong
• Something that worked
• A useful tip

Different people consume content differently.

So I create different types of touchpoints.
↓
8. KEEP THE CONVERSATION GOING
This is one of my favourite things.
Every now and then, after someone has been on my list for a while, I'll send something incredibly simple.
For example:
"Hey Sarah,

How are your gymnastics classes going?"

That's it.

No pitch.

No complicated funnel trick.

Just a genuine question about something I know they're working on.

And surprisingly often, people reply.

They tell me what's going well.

What's not going well.

What they're struggling with.

What they're looking for.

And this is where the "automation" becomes something different.

**The email was automated.

My response isn't.**

If someone takes the time to reply, I reply back.

Suddenly you're not running an email funnel anymore.

You're having a conversation.

I've had some really valuable connections come from emails like this.

People start following what I'm doing more closely.

They reply to future emails.

They ask questions.

They tell me what they're working on.

And over time, they become people who genuinely know, like and trust me.

↓

9. THEN YOU SELL

Eventually, you can make offers.

Evergreen products.

Special offers.

Launches.

Whatever makes sense for your audience.

But I don't immediately start selling.

Personally, I rarely make an offer before someone has received value for at least several days.

People need multiple touchpoints before they're ready to buy.

But everyone is different.

Some people buy quickly.

Others need months.

I've even had people sit on my email list for 4 or 5 years and then suddenly start buying like crazy.

They simply weren't ready before.

That's fine.

The important thing is that you're there when they are ready.

↓

10. FOLLOW UP

Another small thing that can make a big difference:

Unopened emails.

If someone doesn't open an email, it doesn't necessarily mean they're not interested.

Maybe the subject line wasn't good enough.

Some people receive 100 emails a day.

So I'll sometimes resend it with a different subject line.

Same value.

Different hook.

That can recover additional opens and sometimes additional sales.

Small improvements like that compound over time.

↓

11. MAKE IT EVERGREEN

I usually send an email every 5 or 6 days.

And I keep expanding the sequence.

Whenever I have a new idea for a useful email, I simply add it to the end.

The important part:

I make the emails evergreen.

Someone who joins today can receive them.

Someone who joins six months from now can receive them.

Someone who joins two years from now can receive them.

My subscribers can basically spend a year receiving useful content from me.

And all of that keeps running.

↓

THE WHOLE SYSTEM

Traffic

↓

Lead magnet

↓

Email list

↓

Value

↓

Stories

↓

Conversations

↓

Trust

↓

Offers

↓

Sales

And that's basically my entire email marketing strategy.

The funny thing is that once it's built, it requires very little ongoing work.

Your job isn't to constantly sell.

Your job is to keep getting traffic and keep helping people.

If you can keep feeding the top of the funnel, the system keeps working.

And honestly, this is a big part of why I can disappear on holiday and still have sales coming in.

The goal isn't to make money from people.

The goal is to help people.

If your product genuinely solves their problem, they'll happily pay you for it.

That's the business.

If there's enough interest, I can do a proper deep dive into this and show some of the concrete stuff behind it.

Actual emails.

How I structure the sequences.

How I come up with ideas.

How I use storytelling.

How I write subject lines.

How I turn automated emails into real conversations.

What my funnels look like.

And some of the things I've learned from doing this for years.

Would that be useful? Let me know!

They tell me what's going well.

What's not going well.

What they're struggling with.

What they're looking for.

And this is where the "automation" becomes something different.

**The email was automated.

My response isn't.**

If someone takes the time to reply, I reply back.

Suddenly you're not running an email funnel anymore.

You're having a conversation.

I've had some really valuable connections come from emails like this.

People start following what I'm doing more closely.

They reply to future emails.

They ask questions.

They tell me what they're working on.

And over time, they become people who genuinely know, like and trust me.

↓

9. THEN YOU SELL

Eventually, you can make offers.

Evergreen products.

Special offers.

Launches.

Whatever makes sense for your audience.

But I don't immediately start selling.

Personally, I rarely make an offer before someone has received value for at least several days.

People need multiple touchpoints before they're ready to buy.

But everyone is different.

Some people buy quickly.

Others need months.

I've even had people sit on my email list for 4 or 5 years and then suddenly start buying like crazy.

They simply weren't ready before.

That's fine.

The important thing is that you're there when they are ready.

↓

10. FOLLOW UP

Another small thing that can make a big difference:

Unopened emails.

If someone doesn't open an email, it doesn't necessarily mean they're not interested.

Maybe the subject line wasn't good enough.

Some people receive 100 emails a day.

So I'll sometimes resend it with a different subject line.

Same value.

Different hook.

That can recover additional opens and sometimes additional sales.

Small improvements like that compound over time.

↓

11. MAKE IT EVERGREEN

I usually send an email every 5 or 6 days.

And I keep expanding the sequence.

Whenever I have a new idea for a useful email, I simply add it to the end.

The important part:

I make the emails evergreen.

Someone who joins today can receive them.

Someone who joins six months from now can receive them.

Someone who joins two years from now can receive them.

My subscribers can basically spend a year receiving useful content from me.

And all of that keeps running.

↓

THE WHOLE SYSTEM

Traffic

↓

Lead magnet

↓

Email list

↓

Value

↓

Stories

↓

Conversations

↓

Trust

↓

Offers

↓

Sales

And that's basically my entire email marketing strategy.

The funny thing is that once it's built, it requires very little ongoing work.

Your job isn't to constantly sell.

Your job is to keep getting traffic and keep helping people.

If you can keep feeding the top of the funnel, the system keeps working.

And honestly, this is a big part of why I can disappear on holiday and still have sales coming in.

The goal isn't to make money from people.

The goal is to help people.

If your product genuinely solves their problem, they'll happily pay you for it.

That's the business.

If there's enough interest, I can do a proper deep dive into this and show some of the concrete stuff behind it.

Actual emails.

How I structure the sequences.

How I come up with ideas.

How I use storytelling.

How I write subject lines.

How I turn automated emails into real conversations.

What my funnels look like.

And some of the things I've learned from doing this for years.

Would that be useful? Let me know!

WHY INTEL HAS THE POTENTIAL TO BE ONE OF THE NEXT TRILLION DOLLAR COMPANIES $INTC 

The market thinks the AI trade is a GPU story. It's starting to become a CPU story, and Intel is the lead horse for the agentic era.

Look at where the GPU:CPU ratio in AI infrastructure is headed. It's compressing from ~8:1 toward 1:1 or better. Training was GPU-hungry. But agentic workloads (billions of persistent agents making constant, low-latency inference calls) are orchestration-heavy and CPU-bound. As that ratio collapses, a huge amount of value flows back to the CPU layer, and x86 is the default data center architecture on earth. Intel is levered to the exact workload the next decade runs on.

Yet the Street still values INTC as a fading PC-chip company, pricing this quarter's compressed margins and a foundry losing money on its 18A ramp. That's backward-looking. You don't underwrite a franchise on its trough; you underwrite it on the curve it's on.

The foundry is the real trillion-dollar option here. Intel doesn't have to be perfect. It just has to become the credible leading-edge foundry the Western world doesn't have right now. They're already building an external customer book on 18A/14A, and the setup is asymmetric: it takes one anchor customer, a single marquee name committing real volume, to re-rate the entire book overnight. Once one credible player validates the node, everyone else has cover to follow, and the foundry goes from money-losing question mark to strategic asset the Street is forced to reprice.

The yield turnaround is real. When Lip-Bu Tan took over, 18A yields were "not good." The latest data has them jumping from ~65% to 85%+ in a single quarter. Defects aren't a permanent flaw. They're a ramp curve, and it's bending the right way. That's exactly why last quarter's margins finally started expanding, and expanding margins are what turn a beaten-down stock into a growth story.

Then there's the risk the market ignores until it can't: almost all of the world's leading-edge chips get made on one island 100 miles from China. Every hyperscaler, every AI lab, every defense program runs through that single chokepoint. A domestic leading-edge fab is a national security requirement, full stop. That's why the US government took a ~10% stake. Call it what it is, a strategic backstop, not a bailout, and you rarely get to sit on the same side of the table as it.

And the guy running it is Lip-Bu Tan, the most underrated CEO in tech right now. Legendary semis investor, ran Cadence for over a decade, knows basically every fab and frontier customer personally. He's cut the ego projects, driven the yield turnaround, and is aggressively courting outside customers on 18A/14A.

Put it together: the best-positioned name for the agentic CPU shift, a foundry option the market isn't paying for, yields inflecting, margins expanding, real Taiwan tail risk, a government backstop, and an operator who's actually delivering.

The market sees a value trap. I see a $1T company the Street hasn't repriced yet.

Not financial advice.

text:
Monetary policy is already tight enough: wages are beating inflation. That’s real price stability — not 2%.

TLDR: Americans don’t care if inflation is 2% or 5%. They care that wages beat prices. That’s the real definition of price stability — and the only metric that serves both halves of the Fed’s mandate. It’s time for the Fed to modernize its definition of success.

Longer Version: Congress told the Fed to pursue maximum employment and stable prices. It never said 2%. That decimal is a 2012 FOMC invention, not law, and it should be updated to the target people actually care about. Literally nobody budgets in PCE points. Citizens care whether their paychecks are outrunning rent, groceries, and gas. 2% inflation with shrinking real wages is policy failure. 5% with real wages rising faster is policy victory.
Just as a job that doesn’t keep up with the cost of living is not a successful employment outcome, so also the metric that best satisfies the Fed’s mandates is simple: Wages > Inflation.
When pay is beating the cost of living, monetary policy is sufficiently restrictive. The FOMC is crushing demand to hit a number Congress never wrote and is sacrificing households for a target nobody asked for. @SecScottBessent and @realDonaldTrump should insist that the FOMC update its success criteria to target the outcome voters actually care about.

text:
Will the University of Florida simply comply with Florida's public records law, or dig the hole deeper?

On March 26, 2026, I asked UF for its emails about my litigation. Four days later UF's own file recorded 340 pages located: 330 from its IT search, plus 10 with source still unexplained. Over a month later, UF produced 53 pages, every one of them my own emails.

They wrote: "This completes the public records request." That was 135 days ago. They did not reveal the fact that their search revealed those 340 pages and other records until I requested and received metadata related to the original production.

On May 7 a UF attorney asked IT to pull the results for "13th Circuit," my case numbers, "Judge Kelly Ayers, Judge Matthew Felix, and surveillance video" into "a separate pdf." 88 pages. UF has never produced that file, and has never said what is in it.

On September 2 UF's records custodian took the stand. Asked what happened to the 340 pages: "I don't know." Asked whether he or the attorneys decide what gets produced: "Not me."

The court ordered every withheld page delivered for inspection, "every page accounted for." That afternoon UF's lawyer emailed chambers six record files he says total 538 pages. He did not copy me. No custodian has certified what the files are.

There is no index below the file level and no identification of any document within any file. There is no statement, for each record UF claims is exempt, of what it is and why, which section 119.07(1)(e) and (f), Florida Statutes, requires.

So yesterday evening I sent UF's counsel two simple questions. The first, verbatim:

"Are the documents that UF forwarded to the Court precisely the same files that were identified during the initial searches going back to March 30, 2026? Yes ____ No ____ Refuse to answer ____" Basis: ____

The second: prove it, with the native files and their metadata.

UF can show it in an afternoon, and the Court can see what is and is not there. Anything else tells you the University would rather keep fighting than say what it found.

Exhibit A in the images shows just some of the inconsistencies and delays in how @UF and @BrechnerFOI handled the matter. It's absolutely shameful.

And they think they can just continue to play hide the 8-ball and get away with it. This betrayal is at the core of the accountability crisis and endless grift that plague Florida and the US.

SPREAD THIS STORY ABOUT THE MEDIA!! We know, they won't.... https://t.co/ajrQukEyIU

On September 2 UF's records custodian took the stand. Asked what happened to the 340 pages: "I don't know." Asked whether he or the attorneys decide what gets produced: "Not me."

The court ordered every withheld page delivered for inspection, "every page accounted for." That afternoon UF's lawyer emailed chambers six record files he says total 538 pages. He did not copy me. No custodian has certified what the files are.

There is no index below the file level and no identification of any document within any file. There is no statement, for each record UF claims is exempt, of what it is and why, which section 119.07(1)(e) and (f), Florida Statutes, requires.

So yesterday evening I sent UF's counsel two simple questions. The first, verbatim:

"Are the documents that UF forwarded to the Court precisely the same files that were identified during the initial searches going back to March 30, 2026? Yes ____ No ____ Refuse to answer ____" Basis: ____

The second: prove it, with the native files and their metadata.

UF can show it in an afternoon, and the Court can see what is and is not there. Anything else tells you the University would rather keep fighting than say what it found.

Exhibit A in the images shows just some of the inconsistencies and delays in how @UF and @BrechnerFOI handled the matter. It's absolutely shameful.

And they think they can just continue to play hide the 8-ball and get away with it. This betrayal is at the core of the accountability crisis and endless grift that plague Florida and the US.

SPREAD THIS STORY ABOUT THE MEDIA!! We know, they won't.... https://t.co/ajrQukEyIU
